links.note: Asks the aspects of life in which women are disadvantaged - literacy, higher study, low-paid work, wages, safety. That is the disadvantage list, i.e. gender division shaping access to public life and power (24072). 24074 Sexual division of labour is the narrower cause (who does housework), and 24075 is the naturalness claim the answer's first line disposes of in passing.

Stem asks for the FORMS of communal politics with an example each, and the answer walks everyday beliefs, then quest for political dominance, then violence - 24080's description item for item. 24079 is the underlying belief in one religion's superiority, which is what qid:87474 asks.

Caste inequalities persisting - marriage within caste, untouchability not ended, inherited advantage in education and occupation. That is caste as a hereditary division shaping occupation and status (24081), not 24082 which is caste inside electoral politics.

Why caste alone cannot decide elections: no constituency has a single-caste majority, no party takes all of one caste's votes. This is the limits half of the caste-in-politics discussion, so 24082, not 24081 which is the social institution itself.

Women's share in Lok Sabha under 10 per cent and under 5 per cent in state assemblies is the women's-political-representation passage, whose concept in this frame is 24077 (the one-third local-body reservation is that passage's remedy). No separate 'low representation' concept exists here.

The secular-state provisions (no official religion, freedom to profess) are the Constitution's direct answer to communalism, which 24079 defines as using religion as the basis of the nation. FRAME GAP: this chapter's 15 concepts contain no distinct 'secular state' concept, so the secularism items sit on 24079.

The key rejects 'biological difference' and takes 'unequal roles assigned by society' - exactly 24075, which says the division is assumed natural but is produced by society. 24072 states that gender is a social division; this item tests why it is social rather than natural.
Seats reserved for women in Panchayati Raj bodies is 24077's description verbatim; the distractors (Lok Sabha, assemblies, cabinets) are the bodies where no such reservation exists.

Tests the meaning of communal politics: the keyed statements are that one religion is superior and that followers of one religion form one community. That is 24079's definition. 24080 covers how it is expressed, which qid:87467 asks instead.
The wrong statement is that the Constitution gives official status to one religion; the secular-state model is the constitutional answer to communalism (24079). Same frame gap as qid:87471.
'Social divisions based on ____ are peculiar to India' - caste. 24081's description is the only one carrying the unique-to-India claim.

The Civil Rights Movement's dates sit inside the chapter's opening case of a disadvantaged group voicing grievance through democratic politics, which is 24083. A date-recall item takes the concept the event sits in, not a timeline.
Martin Luther King Jr leading the Civil Rights Movement - the same opening case of democratic redress by a marginalised group.
The Black Power movement of 1966 is presented as the more militant companion to the Civil Rights Movement in the same passage on how excluded groups press their claims.

Key is that social divisions become political divisions and lead to conflict - the danger clause, 24084. 24083 is the benign side (grievances voiced and redressed); this item states the explosive outcome.
Britain being predominantly Protestant is from the Northern Ireland case, which the text uses to show class and religion OVERLAPPING and reinforcing each other. That is 24085.
The 1998 peace treaty ending the Nationalists' armed struggle closes the Northern Ireland case in the overlapping-divisions passage, so 24085 rather than 24084.
'Those who feel marginalised, deprived and discriminated have to fight against the injustices; such a fight often takes the democratic path' is 24083's sentence in the text.

The first keyed-true statement, 'social divisions take place when social differences overlap', is 24085's description. Statement 2 (multiple identities) touches 24084 and statement 3's falsity touches the universality passage, but 1 is the load-bearing one.
Peter Norman's human-rights badge at the 1968 Mexico Olympics is the chapter's opening illustration of social division carried into the public arena.
The glossary term African-American is defined inside the same Civil Rights passage; the item is recall of that definition, so it takes that passage's concept.

The key turns on statement 2 being false - identities seen in singular and exclusive terms make accommodation HARD, not easy. That is 24084 word for word. Statements 3 and 4 (constitutional demands, government response) are the other two determinants, which this frame gives no separate concept.

Three of the four statements are the accommodation argument - many small divisions safer than one big one, politics as a force of unity when divisions are expressed, diversity not inherently dangerous - which is 24086. The keyed-false statement (divisions only in countries like India) has no concept in this frame.
India has no official religion - the secular-state provision, which in this frame sits on 24079 (religion as the basis of the nation is what it forbids).

Family laws (marriage, divorce, adoption, inheritance) is the glossary term attached to the women's-movement demand for equality in personal and family life, which is 24076's description. Not 24074, which is about who does the housework.
Incorrect statement is that the secular state reserves seats for religious minorities; the other three are the actual secular provisions. Same secularism cluster on 24079.
Caste hierarchy as a ladder-like ranking of caste groups is the glossary definition of the institution, so 24081. 24082 would need the item to reach elections or candidate selection.

Two of the three keyed ideas - religion-based vote banks and parties promoting religious stereotypes - are the mobilisation and everyday-belief forms in 24080. Only the first (one religion superior) is 24079, so the item's weight is on the forms.

Women's literacy at 54 per cent against men's 76 per cent is from the list of ways women lag behind, i.e. gender division shaping access (24072). NOTE: the options print as 0.54/0.76 etc - percentage formatting was lost on load, though the key is the right value.

High participation of women in public life in Sweden is the counter-case in the public-versus-private passage, so 24073. 24076 Feminist movements is the adjacent sibling, but the item asks about public-life participation, not about the movements.

Patriarchy as a male-dominated system is the name for the power asymmetry 24072 describes (gender division shaping access to public life and power). 24074 is the labour split that expresses it, not the system itself.
Scandinavian countries' high participation of women in public life - the same counter-case as qid:105507, which this item near-duplicates.
